task.goal: Make decisions from a weekly volunteer committee meeting turn into completed actions without making the chair a permanent bottleneck.
hard_constraints: Eight volunteers meet for 45 minutes; no paid project software.
Actions need owners and due dates but members can decline tasks.
Compare completion, rework and volunteer burden over one month.
task.available_resources: Shared notes and a basic calendar.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Consent-based action queue with explicit acceptance
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
The mechanism is a pull system: a committee decision becomes an active commitment only when a volunteer explicitly accepts a bounded task. This prevents apparent agreement from being mistaken for willingness to do the work.

Reserve the last eight minutes of each 45-minute meeting for action acceptance. In shared notes, record each decision’s intended result, smallest useful deliverable, completion criterion and proposed deadline. Invite volunteers to claim tasks; each may decline or negotiate scope and date. Every accepted action receives one owner and a due date. Unclaimed work stays visibly uncommitted, and the committee chooses to defer it, reduce it or abandon it. Nobody receives a task through silence.

Owners add their own calendar reminders and update their rows before the next meeting: completed with evidence, blocked with a specific request, or renegotiation needed. Allow only one active action per person initially. A rotating recorder maintains the queue during the meeting; the chair does not chase updates. Changes affecting the agreed result return to the committee, while owners control execution details.

This needs a shared-note template, calendar access and willingness to leave some decisions unimplemented. It is strongest when unclear commitments and overcommitment cause missed work. It may fail when nobody has capacity or necessary expertise; visibility cannot create either.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: For one month, alternate this method and the committee’s usual assignment method across comparable, low-risk actions. Both require willing owners and due dates. Freeze each action’s original deadline and completion criterion for measurement. Record completion by that deadline, substantive corrections or reopening within seven days, and weekly minutes spent on administration and chasing by each volunteer, including the chair. Report unclaimed work separately so selective acceptance cannot inflate success. Inspect results after four meetings, allowing seven days to observe late rework. The mechanism is challenged if accepted actions perform no better, unclaimed work accumulates, or administration merely shifts from the chair to everyone else. Small samples make findings provisional.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Rotating action steward with limited coordination authority
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
The mechanism is distributed coordination: a different consenting volunteer temporarily holds responsibility for follow-through, supported by explicit authority to resolve routine obstacles. This makes coordination an ordinary committee role rather than an implicit permanent duty of the chair.

During each 45-minute meeting, reserve five minutes to appoint the next week’s steward and review outstanding actions. The steward captures each accepted action in shared notes with its owner, due date, deliverable and completion criterion. Members can decline both tasks and the steward role. An action without an accepting owner remains uncommitted.

Before the meeting ends, identify foreseeable dependencies and authorize a narrow response to each: for example, obtaining an answer from another member or arranging a short discussion. The steward sends one consolidated calendar reminder and offers one brief unblock check during the week. They cannot assign unwilling people, change policy or silently extend deadlines. If an owner withdraws, the steward asks for a replacement or marks the action paused. At the next meeting, the outgoing steward hands unresolved items to the incoming steward through the same notes.

The change in outcome comes from supplying a named coordination function while preventing that function from attaching permanently to one person. It requires several members willing to rotate, access to the shared calendar and clear authority boundaries. It suits work blocked by dependencies more than work blocked by lack of time. Rotation can itself introduce lost context or inconsistent follow-up.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: Over one month, split comparable accepted actions between rotating-steward support and owner-managed follow-through using the same notes template. Agree on the allocation before outcomes are known. Record original-deadline completion, corrections or reopened work within seven days, and each volunteer’s minutes spent executing, coordinating and attending meetings. Count the steward’s handoff time and the chair’s remaining interventions explicitly. Inspect handoffs after each meeting and compare results after four weeks, with seven additional days for rework observation. Reject or simplify the mechanism if coordination time increases without better completion, handoffs repeatedly lose information, or the chair still resolves most obstacles. A small trial cannot establish long-term willingness to rotate.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Protected execution time inside the weekly meeting
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
The mechanism is to replace some discussion with immediate execution. Instead of relying entirely on volunteers finding additional time later, the committee uses part of its existing shared time to finish small actions or produce inspectable first steps.

Structure the 45 minutes as five minutes reviewing prior actions, twenty minutes making decisions, fifteen minutes doing selected work and five minutes recording outcomes. For each decision selected for execution, define a useful deliverable that fits the work period: draft an announcement, prepare a purchasing list or complete an application section. One volunteer explicitly accepts ownership and a due date, which can be the meeting’s end. Others may help or decline; declining does not create a later obligation. Members without a suitable action can review shared materials or finish their participation early.

Use shared notes as the work surface and record links or text showing what was produced. Where work continues afterward, retain one consenting owner, a due date and a clear remaining step, with a calendar reminder. Reviewers check completed outputs against the agreed criterion during the next meeting. Facilitation and note-taking rotate among willing members, so the chair need not organize separate work sessions or chase everyone.

This requires actions that can be divided into meaningful short units and a committee willing to reduce discussion time. It could work because starting costs, clarification and access to colleagues are handled while everyone is present. It is less suitable for confidential work, physical errands or tasks awaiting outside responses. The main risk is displacing necessary decisions.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: For four weeks, alternate protected-execution meetings with the usual 45-minute format. Track all decisions and resulting accepted actions, including complex work that cannot fit a sprint. Compare original-deadline completion, substantive corrections within seven days, and total meeting, execution and coordination minutes per volunteer. Also record agenda items deferred because discussion time ran out. Inspect actual outputs rather than counting work started as work completed. Allow seven days after the final meeting to observe rework. The approach is challenged if it produces only trivial completions, defers important decisions, or fails to reduce outside-meeting burden. Differences between weekly agendas will limit causal confidence.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Bounded authority to finish without further approval
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
The mechanism is to remove repeat approval as a cause of stalled work. When the committee makes a decision, it also gives the accepting owner enough authority to complete it within explicit boundaries. The chair stops being the default approver for execution details.

Use six minutes of each 45-minute meeting to finalize action mandates in shared notes. Each mandate states the intended result, one consenting owner, a due date, observable completion criteria, permitted discretion and any limits on expenditure or external commitments. Members may decline or negotiate the task. Work without an accepting owner remains uncommitted. For example, an owner could publish a routine notice using agreed facts and a specified audience without returning for approval of every sentence.

An owner may act within the mandate and mark completion with evidence in the notes. Only a boundary-crossing change requires another committee decision; record that question for the next meeting rather than routing ordinary choices through the chair. Legally required approvals and existing financial controls remain applicable. Owners set their own calendar reminders, and a consenting recorder captures mandates during the meeting.

This requires trust, sufficiently clear decisions and tasks for which the committee can delegate execution authority. It could improve completion when volunteers wait for reassurance or repeated sign-off. It cannot solve insufficient capacity, and vague boundaries could increase rework. Its suitability is uncertain until the committee checks whether approval delays actually occur.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: For four weeks, allocate comparable, low-risk accepted actions between bounded mandates and the committee’s usual approval process. Both groups have willing owners, due dates and completion criteria. Record completion by the original deadline, approval-related waiting days, substantive corrections or reopening observed during the month, and each volunteer’s execution and administration minutes, including the chair’s. Count mandate-writing time within meeting burden. Compare actions with equal observation time and flag late-month actions whose rework remains unobserved. The mechanism is challenged if approval waiting falls without better completion, corrections rise, or drafting boundaries consumes more volunteer time than it saves. A small trial provides directional evidence only.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Book the work when accepting the action
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
The mechanism is to convert a general intention into a specific appointment with the work. An accepted action gets both a delivery deadline and an owner-chosen execution slot, reducing reliance on remembering the task and finding spare time later.

Reserve six minutes within each 45-minute meeting for action planning. Record each action’s deliverable, completion criterion, consenting owner and due date in shared notes. Members may decline. Before accepting, the prospective owner identifies a realistic calendar slot before the deadline and a concrete first step: for example, Wednesday at 19:00, open the venue list and request availability from three venues. The owner puts the appointment in their basic calendar; shared notes need only show that a slot exists, not disclose private calendar details.

If the work needs several sessions, the owner books enough time for the estimated effort or reduces the promised scope before accepting. They identify one predictable obstacle and a fallback, such as a second slot if childcare disrupts the first. If a slot is missed, the owner reschedules before the deadline or marks the commitment at risk in the notes. The committee handles unresolved risks during its next scheduled review; the chair does not maintain a separate reminder service.

This needs calendar access, reasonably predictable availability and tasks whose effort can be estimated roughly. It could work when willingness exists but intentions repeatedly lose out to competing demands. It offers little help with missing expertise or external dependencies. Calendar entries are planning aids, not evidence of progress, and volunteers must remain free to decline rather than invent unrealistic availability.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: Over one month, allocate comparable accepted actions between calendar booking and a simple owner-plus-deadline list. Keep completion criteria and review time equivalent. Record original-deadline completion, substantive rework observed during the month, and weekly execution, planning and chasing minutes for every volunteer. Record missed appointments and rescheduling time without collecting private calendar details. Compare rework only across equal observation windows and identify actions still too recent to assess. The mechanism is challenged if appointments are routinely missed, completion does not improve, or scheduling burden outweighs reduced chasing. Inspect actual deliverables; a booked or attended slot does not count as completion.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Consenting backup pairs for continuity when availability changes
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
The mechanism is continuity through a prearranged backup: an action can survive its owner's unexpected loss of availability without waiting for the chair to find a replacement. This could help when volunteers intend to deliver but personal commitments disrupt execution.

Reserve seven minutes of the existing 45-minute meeting to arrange coverage for selected actions. In shared notes, record the deliverable, completion criterion, accepting owner, due date and a consenting backup. Either person may decline. The backup accepts a specific, limited rescue contribution, such as finishing a draft from existing notes, rather than an unlimited obligation to complete whatever remains.

At an agreed checkpoint before the deadline, the owner records completed work and whether help is needed. If the owner requests a handoff, or misses the checkpoint, the backup checks the notes and confirms whether they can take ownership. Transfer is explicit; silence never creates an obligation. If neither person has capacity, mark the action at risk for committee review. A short progress note makes transfer possible without the chair reconstructing events. Calendar reminders go to the pair.

This needs overlapping skills, some spare capacity and work that can be handed over safely. Begin with at most one backup commitment per member. Confidential or specialist actions may be unsuitable. The main uncertainty is whether backup coverage supplies useful resilience or merely reserves scarce volunteer time twice.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: For one month, allocate comparable, transferable actions between backup coverage and a simple consenting-owner-plus-deadline list. Use the same completion criteria. Compare completion by original deadlines, substantive corrections within seven days of delivery, and each volunteer's weekly execution and coordination minutes, including backup preparation and chair intervention. Inspect late-month deliveries only for the rework window actually observed. Record whether handoffs occurred and succeeded. Coverage is challenged if disrupted actions still stall, or any completion benefit requires disproportionate standby and handoff effort. If no availability disruptions occur, the trial cannot meaningfully test the proposed mechanism.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Recipient verification before an action is counted complete
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
The mechanism is a direct feedback loop between the person producing an output and the person who will use it. Completion means the output is usable for its agreed purpose, reducing work that appears finished in meeting notes but later needs correction or another chair-mediated discussion.

Within six minutes of each 45-minute meeting, record each selected action's consenting owner, due date and intended recipient in shared notes. The recipient may be another committee member who needs the result for a subsequent step. Both roles are voluntary. Together they write one observable acceptance check: for example, a venue comparison includes availability, total cost and accessibility information sufficient to choose a venue.

The owner posts the output directly in the notes. The recipient checks it by an agreed review deadline and either confirms acceptance or identifies the specific unmet criterion. The owner handles corrections directly with the recipient. New preferences beyond the agreed criterion become a separate committee request rather than silently expanding the task. Silence leaves the output marked 'delivered, awaiting verification'; it does not imply acceptance. The chair has no routine sign-off role.

This requires an identifiable user of the output, reviewers with relevant knowledge and willingness to give brief feedback. Use it only where usability can be checked cheaply. It could reduce ambiguous completion and downstream rework, but it adds review effort and can create a new bottleneck if recipients lack capacity. Shared notes and calendar reminders are sufficient.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: Over one month, allocate comparable actions between recipient verification and owner-declared completion, with willing owners, due dates and written criteria in both groups. Compare usable outputs delivered by the original deadline, substantive correction cycles, and each volunteer's execution, review and coordination minutes. At the next meeting, briefly inspect outputs from both groups against their criteria so self-declared completion does not automatically score better. Count this inspection burden. Track review delays and chair interventions separately. Compare rework within equal seven-day windows and flag incomplete observation. The mechanism is challenged if verification delays completion without reducing unusable outputs or later corrections. Small numbers and reviewers influencing both groups limit confidence.

EXPAND.title: Delegate bounded decisions to the person who can execute them
EXPAND.proposal:
The mechanism is to remove a separate committee approval step for routine work. A volunteer who must return next week for small execution choices can lose most of the available week even after accepting the action.

At the first meeting, spend up to ten of the 45 minutes defining a narrow delegation for recurring, low-risk decisions: the intended outcome, permitted choices, existing resource limits and conditions requiring committee approval. A willing volunteer accepts both the decision authority and a dated deliverable. Members may decline; work without an accepting owner stays deferred. Record the delegation in shared notes and put its expiry in the basic calendar.

Within those boundaries, the owner chooses and executes without waiting for the chair. They record the choice and evidence of completion in the notes. For example, an owner may select an announcement’s wording and publication time within an agreed audience and date window. Spending, public commitments or policy changes outside the written boundary return to the committee. When a boundary is reached, the owner continues any useful authorized work and records the specific decision needed. The next meeting resolves that exception or reduces the scope.

This needs volunteers with relevant access and judgment, plus committee willingness to accept different reasonable choices. It adds no coordinator role. It could shorten delay where repeated approvals are the obstacle; it will do little where owners lack time. Poorly chosen boundaries could shift delay into correction or create unwanted commitments.
EXPAND.experiment: A consenting trial recorder maintains the comparison for one month. Allocate comparable, low-risk actions between bounded delegation and the prior explicit-acceptance queue, which leaves execution choices subject to existing approval practice. Both use willing owners, original due dates and fixed completion criteria. Compare on-time completion, substantive rework within seven days, and each volunteer’s meeting, execution and coordination minutes, including the chair’s. Record time waiting for approval and any boundary breaches. Stop a delegation immediately after an unauthorized external commitment; stop expanding the trial if correction time exceeds approval time saved. Review after four weeks, allowing seven days for final rework observation. No improvement after counting boundary-setting and correction work would favor the simpler acceptance queue; the small sample remains provisional.

EXPAND.title: Require executable inputs before starting the deadline
EXPAND.proposal:
The mechanism is to prevent commitments from entering execution without the information, access or materials required to finish them. An accepted task can otherwise sit idle while its owner discovers missing permissions or an unanswered factual question.

Reserve seven minutes of each 45-minute meeting for a readiness check. For each proposed action, work backward from the deliverable and identify only indispensable inputs: a recipient, an existing document, permission to edit, an agreed factual answer or a response from another person. Verify these in the shared notes where possible. Avoid turning the check into a full project plan.

If inputs are available, a willing owner accepts the deliverable and due date, records the relevant links and sets a calendar reminder. If an input is missing, create a separate, dated preparation action with a consenting owner; mark the intended delivery visibly blocked and preserve its desired completion date. Nobody receives either task by default. When preparation finishes, the prospective delivery owner explicitly accepts a feasible deadline. If nobody can obtain the input, the committee reduces, defers or drops the work at its next meeting.

Owners report completion evidence directly in the notes. Newly discovered prerequisites follow the same preparation path, without chair chasing. This requires honest identification of minimum inputs and volunteers able to supply them. It should help when hidden dependencies cause delay, but cannot create missing access or outside cooperation. Excessive checking could delay straightforward work or improve reported completion merely by postponing commitments.
EXPAND.experiment: A willing trial recorder compares readiness checking with the prior explicit-acceptance queue on comparable actions for one month. Track every proposed delivery from its original decision date, including blocked and unclaimed work. Compare delivery by its initially desired date, completion by accepted deadlines, substantive rework within seven days, and preparation, execution and coordination minutes for all eight volunteers. Inspect the first few prerequisite lists for unnecessary checks. Stop adding the gate if two successive checks consume time without discovering a dependency that would prevent delivery; simplify immediately if preparation tasks crowd out delivery. The approach loses if its better accepted-task completion disappears when blocked work and preparation burden are included. Finish with a seven-day rework observation window; differences in task difficulty limit confidence.

EXPAND.title: Use a downstream receiver to define and accept the handoff
EXPAND.proposal:
The mechanism is to make usability explicit before work starts and verify it where the result will actually be used. A task can be marked complete yet require substantial repair because its producer and recipient imagined different outputs.

For actions with an identifiable user, reserve up to seven minutes within the 45-minute meeting for the owner and a willing receiver to agree on a short acceptance example. Record the deliverable, essential content, destination and a concrete condition for use in shared notes. For a venue shortlist, for example, the receiver may need availability and total cost for the agreed date, rather than a list of names. Keep the criteria limited to what enables the next step.

The action owner explicitly accepts a due date; the receiver separately accepts a review date. Either can decline. If no receiver accepts, use ordinary owner reporting and mark the action outside this trial. The owner delivers through the notes, and the receiver checks against the recorded criteria. They either acknowledge that the result is usable or identify a specific unmet criterion. The owner accepts a repair date or declines further work, leaving the unresolved handoff visible for the next meeting. New preferences require a new committee decision rather than silently expanding the original obligation.

This needs someone who understands downstream use and can review promptly. Calendar reminders belong to the two volunteers, so acceptance does not depend on the chair. It may reduce rework and premature closure, but can create a new reviewer bottleneck or encourage overly detailed specifications.
EXPAND.experiment: A consenting trial recorder pairs comparable handoff tasks for one month: receiver acceptance versus the prior explicit-acceptance queue with owner-reported completion. Fix criteria and original deadlines before execution. Compare usable delivery by the original deadline, substantive corrections or reopening within seven days, and all volunteers’ specification, production, review and coordination minutes. Record reviewer waiting time and disputed additions separately. Inspect one actual handoff after the first week. Stop assigning new receiver reviews if two reviews miss their agreed dates or review effort exceeds the repair work it plausibly prevents. Retain the method only if usable completion or rework improves enough to justify the added burden. Observe final deliveries for seven additional days; a small set of different deliverables cannot establish a reliable effect.

EXPAND.title: Preauthorize a limited fallback when an owner becomes unavailable
EXPAND.proposal:
The mechanism is recovery through reserved backup capacity. An explicit commitment can still fail when a volunteer becomes unexpectedly unavailable; waiting until the next meeting to discover the problem leaves no recovery time.

Use up to seven minutes of each 45-minute meeting to identify a small number of time-sensitive actions for backup coverage. Each action needs a consenting primary owner, original due date and clear completion criterion. A second volunteer may explicitly accept a narrowly defined fallback, including its maximum scope and activation date. Both roles are optional. Start with at most two covered actions and one backup commitment per person so the committee does not promise its entire capacity twice.

Keep working material in the shared notes from the start. Before the deadline, set a checkpoint that leaves enough time for the fallback. At that checkpoint, the primary records either a usable result or a request to activate the backup. If no update appears by the agreed cutoff, the written agreement authorizes the backup to proceed and requires the primary to pause duplicate work. The backup checks the notes, records activation and completes only the agreed fallback. This might be sending a minimum viable announcement, not recreating an entire campaign.

The fallback must itself have a due date and useful completion criterion. If the backup also becomes unavailable, they record that immediately; the committee must reduce or defer the action. Nobody automatically inherits it, including the chair.

This needs spare capacity, shared work access and tasks with safe handoffs. It can reduce disruption from absence, but reserved capacity, duplicate effort and lower-quality fallback outputs may outweigh the benefit.
EXPAND.experiment: A willing trial recorder compares covered actions with similarly urgent actions using the prior owner-managed acceptance queue over one month. Allocate coverage before knowing which owners will become unavailable. Compare completion by original deadlines, substantive rework within seven days, and each volunteer’s execution, checkpoint, handoff and coordination minutes. Also record reserved backup capacity, actual activations and duplicate work; report whether any real interruption occurred. Inspect the first activation directly. Stop new coverage if a handoff causes conflicting external actions or backup obligations exceed the agreed capacity limit. The mechanism offers no demonstrated benefit if completion is unchanged while reservation or handoff burden rises. Allow seven days after the month for rework observation; no interruptions would leave its recovery value untested.

EXPAND.title: Accepted action queue with explicit withdrawal and release
EXPAND.proposal:
Upgrade of the consent-based action queue: retain explicit acceptance, bounded deliverables, completion criteria, due dates and an initial limit of one active action per person. Add a withdrawal procedure so an interrupted commitment does not remain silently assigned or default to the chair.

Reserve eight minutes of each 45-minute meeting for the queue. A rotating, consenting recorder captures commitments in shared notes. Members may decline or negotiate any task; unclaimed work is reduced, deferred or dropped. Owners set their own calendar reminders and post completion evidence or a specific blocker before the next meeting.

The changed action is an explicit release rule. An owner who cannot continue marks the action 'replacement needed' and records the usable work and remaining step. They retain responsibility only for that brief handoff, not for finding a successor or finishing work they have declined. Transfer occurs only when another volunteer records acceptance and a feasible due date. Until then, the action is visibly paused. A missed deadline without an update also moves it to paused at the next meeting; nobody silently inherits it. The committee then reoffers, reduces or drops it within the existing queue review. Preserve original deadlines for measurement.

This needs shared notes, personal calendar reminders and willingness to abandon unsupported commitments. Compared with the original queue, it makes interruption recoverable without chair chasing, at the cost of occasional handoff notes and paused work. It cannot rescue urgent tasks between meetings when nobody is available; use it first for work where a week's delay is tolerable.
EXPAND.experiment: A willing recorder runs a four-meeting trial, assigning comparable, nonurgent actions to the original acceptance queue or the queue with explicit release. Both require consenting owners and due dates. Count all proposed work, including unclaimed and paused actions. Compare completion by original deadlines, substantive rework within seven days, and each volunteer's execution, administration and chasing minutes, including the chair's. Record interruptions, time awaiting replacement and handoff effort. In week one, inspect a hypothetical owner withdrawal to check that responsibility is clear without requiring a real failure. Stop adding the release procedure if transfers repeatedly produce duplicate work; leave affected work paused until the committee resolves ownership. Retain it only if recovery or clarity justifies its added burden. Observe final deliveries for seven additional days; without real interruptions, recovery benefits remain uncertain.

EXPAND.title: Bounded delegation with a preagreed response to exceptions
EXPAND.proposal:
Upgrade of bounded decision delegation: preserve owner authority over routine execution, written limits, willing acceptance, dated deliverables, recorded choices and expiry. Close the gap where an owner reaches a boundary between meetings and useful work otherwise stalls while awaiting approval.

At the first 45-minute meeting, use up to ten minutes to define narrow delegations for recurring, low-risk work. For each, the committee records the outcome, permitted choices, existing resource limits and conditions requiring approval. A volunteer may decline. Only proceed when the owner has the necessary access and accepts a due date.

The changed action is for the committee to choose a safe exception response when granting the delegation: either a specifically authorized reduced deliverable or a pause if no useful reduced deliverable exists. For example, if a publication fact cannot be verified, an owner may omit that optional claim when the committee has explicitly authorized omission; otherwise publication pauses. This does not authorize spending, policy changes or external commitments beyond the written boundary.

The owner records the triggering evidence and applies that response without chair approval. If the reduced deliverable also becomes infeasible, the owner stops that portion and records the precise question for the next meeting. The committee decides whether to amend, withdraw or renew authority during a five-minute exception review. Expiry ends authority unless renewed.

This uses shared notes and calendar expiry reminders. It requires the committee to identify a useful safe response in advance; if it cannot, ordinary committee approval remains the fallback. Compared with the original delegation, it may avoid unnecessary waiting but adds boundary-setting effort and risks delivering less than intended. It will not help owners who lack execution time.
EXPAND.experiment: A consenting recorder compares ordinary bounded delegation with delegation containing an explicit exception response over one month, using comparable low-risk actions. Fix original deadlines and completion criteria; report reduced deliveries separately unless they meet those original criteria. Compare original-deadline completion, substantive corrections within seven days, and every volunteer's execution, boundary-setting, coordination and meeting minutes. Record approval waiting, exception uses and unauthorized actions. Inspect the first exception against its recorded authority. Stop the affected delegation immediately after a boundary breach or an unusable fallback; return it to committee approval. Retain the addition only if useful delivery or waiting improves enough to justify specification and correction effort. Allow seven days after the month for rework observation. Few exceptions would leave its benefit uncertain.

EXPAND.title: Standing recurring commitments instead of weekly reassignment
EXPAND.proposal:
The new mechanism is continuity: for genuinely repeated work, replace weekly conversion of the same decision into a new assignment with a short, expiring service commitment. This removes repeated assignment and negotiation rather than adding follow-up coordination.

During the first meeting, spend at most eight minutes identifying one or two recurring outputs already wanted by the committee, such as a weekly attendance summary. A volunteer may accept responsibility for four dated occurrences, negotiate fewer occurrences or decline. Record each occurrence's due date, the common completion criterion, required inputs and a link to the reusable output format in shared notes. Put the occurrences and the commitment's expiry in the basic calendar. This grants no new decision authority.

The owner produces each occurrence and adds completion evidence directly. Subsequent meetings spend at most three minutes on exceptions, rather than reassigning the routine. The owner may withdraw from future occurrences at any time by marking them uncommitted. Already accepted occurrences may also be declined; record their status explicitly. There is no automatic replacement or renewal. The committee uses the exception review to seek a consenting replacement, reduce frequency or suspend the routine. If required inputs are missing, the owner records the missing input and pauses that occurrence rather than producing unsupported work. Changed requirements require renewed acceptance.

This needs stable recurring demand, a volunteer with capacity, shared notes and a basic calendar. Compared with weekly assignment, it could reduce repeated negotiation and preserve working context. It also concentrates work and can perpetuate an unnecessary routine, so the commitment expires after one month and counts against the volunteer's available capacity. Where demand or capacity is unstable, use individual accepted actions instead.
EXPAND.experiment: A willing recorder selects two roughly comparable existing routines for a four-week trial: one uses a standing commitment, the other weekly explicit acceptance. Do not create extra work merely to test the method. Compare useful occurrences completed by their original due dates, substantive rework within seven days, and each volunteer's meeting, execution and coordination minutes, including the chair's. Count skipped, unclaimed and withdrawn occurrences, and record whether each output was actually used. Review after two weeks: suspend a routine if its output is no longer needed, and revert to weekly acceptance if the owner reports that the standing commitment exceeds their capacity. At month end, compare completion and burden before considering renewal, with seven further days to observe rework. If no suitable repeated work exists, this route is inapplicable; differences between routines limit causal conclusions.
